passage: After Saturday swimming class at the sports club, the girls' changing room echoed like a well. Lakshmi, the newest, came out in a big frilly costume and orange armbands. Someone said, "Quack quack," and then six girls were quacking and flapping their elbows. Bidisha, ten, quacked too, loud, her voice lost among the others. It didn't feel like her; it felt like the room. Lakshmi pulled a towel round herself and sat on the bench. On Monday the coach paired Bidisha and Lakshmi for kicking practice, just the two of them at the shallow end. Bidisha couldn't look at her. Halfway through, she held out her spare goggles. "These don't leak," she mumbled.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi wearing when she came out?
qa.a: She came out in a big frilly costume and orange armbands.

qa.q: Why did quacking in the changing room not feel like Bidisha's own act?
qa.a: Her voice was lost among six others, so she felt the room was doing it, not her, and nobody would single her out.

qa.q: What turning point shows Bidisha she would never have teased Lakshmi alone?
qa.a: When the coach paired them at the shallow end, she could not even look at Lakshmi, so she offered her spare goggles instead.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt sitting on the bench with the towel round her?
qa.a: As the newest girl, she probably felt humiliated and alone against a whole room, with nobody in particular to answer.

grounding: A ten-year-old joins a group's teasing in a changing room that she would never do alone, because her voice feels lost in the crowd.

passage: I'm Lavanya, Charu's older sister. This was our cousin's wedding. Little Mohit had come in his father's kurta, which reached his ankles. About twelve of us cousins crowded round him. Someone whispered, "Tent!" and then everyone was chanting it. Charu, nine, who usually hands sweets to the smallest children, chanted loudest, clapping. Mohit stood holding the hem of the kurta. Then the band stopped all at once, and in the silence one voice rang out: "TENT!" It was Charu's. A hundred heads turned. I watched her face go from pink to white. She ran to Mohit and straightened his kurta sleeve, as if that could undo it. I don't know what she felt, but she stayed by him all evening.

qa.q: Why did Mohit's kurta reach his ankles?
qa.a: He had come in his father's kurta.

qa.q: What does Charu's face going from pink to white suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was shocked and ashamed once her voice was heard alone, because in the crowd the chant had not felt like hers.

qa.q: What did Charu do after the moment of silence, and was it a good choice?
qa.a: She went straight to Mohit and stayed by his side all evening, which was a kind way to show she was sorry, though saying sorry aloud would also help.

qa.q: What was the teasing like for Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit faced twelve children at once and could only stand holding the hem of the kurta, with no single person to stop.

grounding: A usually kind nine-year-old chants a cruel nickname with a crowd of cousins, and is shaken when her voice is heard alone.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage:
Dear Rajni,

I'm writing this instead of saying it, because I'm a coward about saying it.

Last Friday, when the anonymous school confessions page posted the clip of you singing at the assembly, the comments were already crazy. Hundreds. Everyone was adding something. I scrolled for ten minutes and then I added one too, under a made-up name. It was mean. I won't repeat it.

I keep trying to explain how it felt. It didn't feel like me typing. You felt far away, like a picture, and everyone else was doing it, so it seemed like just one more drop in the rain. But it was my thumb. On Monday I saw you eat lunch alone in the library, and I knew which drop was mine.

I've deleted it. I'm sorry. Your high note was actually good.

Jasleen (the girl two rows behind you in maths)

qa.q: Where did Jasleen see Rajni eating lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Jasleen saw Rajni eat lunch alone in the library.

qa.q: Why did posting the comment not feel like her own action to Jasleen at the time?
qa.a: Rajni felt far away like a picture, the name was made up and everyone else was commenting, so it felt like one more drop in the rain.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen make after Monday, and what could she add to it?
qa.a: She deleted the comment and wrote to apologise; she could also report the clip to a teacher so the page takes it down.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rajni may feel a mix of hurt and relief, hurt to know a classmate joined in, but glad someone admitted it and praised Rajni's high note.

grounding: A teenager joins a cruel comment pile-on under a made-up name because the target feels distant and everyone is doing it, and later owns it.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: "You want the embarrassing one, Aadhya? Fine, this is Yash at his worst. Last year I played this online shooting game every night in a voice lobby, all random usernames, nobody's real face. One night a player on our team kept dying early. Someone started calling him useless, then another person, then all five of us. I joined in. I said things I would never say to anyone at school, and it felt like nothing, like I was just part of the noise and he was just a username. Then he unmuted to reply and his voice cracked. He sounded about twelve. He said, 'Sorry, I'm new.' Everyone laughed and kept going. I left the game. I sat there with my headset in my lap feeling sick. The worst part? For those ten minutes, I honestly hadn't felt like it was me."

qa.q: How many people in the lobby were calling the player useless?
qa.a: All five of them, including Yash, were calling him useless.

qa.q: What made Yash feel sick with the headset in his lap?
qa.a: Hearing the player's cracked, young-sounding voice made the target suddenly real, and Yash realised the cruelty had been his even though it felt like just noise.

qa.q: What could Yash do the next time a lobby starts piling on someone?
qa.a: He could stay quiet or say one plain line such as 'leave him, he's new,' and mute or report the players who keep going, instead of joining in.

qa.q: What was that night like for the new player?
qa.a: He was a young beginner who apologised and was laughed at by five strangers at once, with no one to reason with.

grounding: A teenager in an anonymous gaming lobby joins a pile-on because everyone is doing it and the target feels distant, and only later feels it was his.

passage: The house football final ended with Vishal's own goal. By the time he reached the corridor, it was full: thirty, maybe forty students from Tagore House, all shouting at once. "Traitor!" "Who even picked him?" Someone kicked his bag along the floor. Vishal, fourteen, turned to answer one boy, and three others shouted over him from behind. Every face was a different face. There was nobody to explain it to. His chest went tight and his ears roared. Usha, from his class, slipped out and ran for the games teacher. Mr Dsouza came at once, cleared the corridor in a minute and sat with Vishal on the stairs. "It was one bad bounce, and none of this is your fault," he said. He walked Vishal to the counsellor's room himself and phoned his mother before the last bell.

qa.q: How did the house football final end for Vishal?
qa.a: It ended with Vishal's own goal.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he tried to answer one boy and others shouted from behind?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and trapped, because there was no single person to reason with, which made his chest tight and his ears roar.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference for Vishal, and why?
qa.a: Usha running for the teacher brought an adult at once, and Mr Dsouza cleared the crowd, stayed with Vishal and took it to the counsellor and his mother that same day.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt watching the crowd close in on Vishal?
qa.a: Usha was probably frightened for him, and knowing one student could not stop forty, chose to fetch an adult quickly.

grounding: A teenager mobbed by a hostile crowd after a match is overwhelmed because there is no one person to reason with, and a teacher steps in the same day.

passage:
To: Mr Hemant Rao, school counsellor
Subject: I don't know what to do

Sir,

Since yesterday someone made an account using my photo and posted that I cheated in the science exam. Now there are more than two hundred comments. Most are from accounts with no real names. People I don't know are messaging me. Every time I delete one, five more come. I tried replying to one to explain, but I can't explain to two hundred people. I haven't slept. I didn't go to school today.

Raghav, Class 10B

Reply, 4:40 pm same day:

Raghav, thank you for telling me, beta. None of this is your fault. Please don't reply to any of them. Take screenshots and keep them. I have just spoken to your mother on the phone; she is on her way home to be with you. I have reported the account to the principal, and we will meet with both of you first thing tomorrow.

Mr Rao

qa.q: How many comments were there on the post about Raghav?
qa.a: There were more than two hundred comments.

qa.q: Why did Raghav feel he could not explain himself?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed because the comments came from hundreds of nameless accounts, so there was no single person to explain to.

qa.q: Which steps in Mr Rao's reply help Raghav most?
qa.a: He tells Raghav it is not his fault, says not to reply, asks for screenshots, calls his mother that day and reports the account to the principal.

qa.q: How might Raghav's mother feel after the counsellor's phone call?
qa.a: She would likely be worried and upset for her son, but relieved that the school acted quickly and that she can be home with him.

grounding: A student mobbed by hundreds of anonymous comments feels overwhelmed with no one to reason with, and a counsellor responds the same day.

passage:
Coach's note, 3 February. Written by Kamal, women's hockey coach.

We won the inter-college final today, and I'm writing this down because of what Arohi, our twenty-year-old centre half, did afterwards. The team piled into the stadium car park to celebrate. Music, dancing, all good. Around seven someone brought out a big bag of firecrackers, and within ten minutes girls were throwing lit crackers at each other's feet, and two were climbing the team bus to set off rockets from the roof. People were laughing in a way that didn't sound like them. Arohi saw it early. She took the cracker bag, handed it to me, and called the team into a circle for a photo with the trophy, away from the bus. They came. Nobody got hurt.

My next step: I've thanked Arohi in front of the team and asked her to help plan how we celebrate next time.

qa.q: What were two players climbing to set off rockets?
qa.a: They were climbing the team bus to set off rockets from the roof.

qa.q: What did Arohi seem to notice about her teammates' mood?
qa.a: She noticed the celebration had turned reckless, with people laughing in a way that did not sound like them, and seemed to sense they would regret it.

qa.q: Why was calling the team for a trophy photo a smart move?
qa.a: It gave everyone a happy reason to step away from the bus and the crackers without scolding anyone, so the mood calmed quickly.

qa.q: How might the players who were throwing crackers see it the next day?
qa.a: They may feel embarrassed and relieved, realising how close someone came to getting hurt at a happy moment.

grounding: A young player notices a victory celebration sliding from festive to reckless and calmly moves her team away before anyone gets hurt.

subtype: Noticing the slide in a group [Observer]
passage:
Sunday, very late.

India won the final tonight and the whole city came out. Minakshi and I went down to the big crossing near our girls' PG with our faces painted. For the first hour it was lovely: strangers hugging, drums, people handing out sweets.

Then it changed. Some boys started rocking a stopped bus with people still inside. Others climbed a traffic signal. A group was shaking a scooter while the rider begged them to stop, and people were filming instead of helping. The cheering got a hard edge. I looked at Minakshi and she was cheering at the bus too, without seeming to notice.

I thought: tomorrow half these people will see those videos and feel sick.

I said, "Let's go, now," and pulled her into a side lane. From the gate I called the police helpline about the bus. Minakshi kept saying, "It was just fun." At home she went quiet.

- Sharmila

qa.q: What were some boys doing to the stopped bus?
qa.a: They were rocking it with people still inside.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking when she saw the crowd change?
qa.a: She was thinking that many of these people would see the videos tomorrow and feel sick, so she knew the fun had turned into something they would regret.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do once she saw the mood shift, and why did timing matter?
qa.a: She left at once with Minakshi and called the police helpline about the bus; acting early meant they were out before the crowd got worse.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see the evening once she goes quiet at home?
qa.a: Minakshi may be starting to realise she was swept along, cheering at something she would never support on her own.

grounding: A young woman at a victory celebration sees the mood turn reckless, understands people will regret it, and leaves with her friend and alerts help.

passage:
HR note, 22 May. Written by Suraj, people team.

The anonymous survey on the new floor manager got forty comments, many harsh and personal. Several matched word for word, and I later learned a group chat had drafted them together as a joke.

One entry stood out: it was signed. Wasim, twenty-five, from dispatch, had written his own comment and put his name at the bottom. He said the manager's shift changes were hard on people with long commutes, gave two examples, suggested a fix. When I asked him why he'd signed an anonymous form, he said, "My name goes wherever my words go, form or no form. If I wouldn't say it to her face, I shouldn't write it." He also told me he had left the group chat when the jokes started getting personal.

My next step: share Wasim's specific points with the manager, and remind all teams the survey is for fair feedback, not insults.

qa.q: How many comments did the anonymous survey get?
qa.a: It got forty comments.

qa.q: What does Wasim's reason for signing the form show about how he feels about his words?
qa.a: He feels responsible for his words even when nobody can see him, and comfortable writing only what he would say to the manager's face.

qa.q: Which of Wasim's choices protected both the manager and the feedback?
qa.a: Leaving the group chat when the jokes turned personal and writing specific, signed points meant the real problem was heard without joining the pile-on.

qa.q: How might the floor manager feel reading Wasim's comment next to the others?
qa.a: She might feel stung by the harsh ones, but able to take Wasim's signed, fair comment seriously and act on it.

grounding: A young employee signs his own honest feedback and leaves a group chat drafting harsh anonymous comments, staying accountable even when unseen.

subtype: Keeping the self in the crowd [Response]
passage:
Saturday night

Corporate cricket today, our office against the bank team. By the fifteenth over our lot on the boundary were sledging their bowler, a heavy, sweet guy called Santosh. Jokes about his weight, louder each over, everyone laughing, everyone joining. I heard my own mouth start one of the chants. I stopped halfway.

Nobody would have picked out my voice. But I kept thinking, it's still my voice. I'd carry that chant home with me.

So I said what I actually meant: "Good ball, bowler!" "Whose side are you on, bhai?" Deepak asked. When the chant started again, I walked off to field at long-on, away from them.

After the match I found Santosh at the water cooler and said, "Sorry about our boundary. That wasn't cricket." He shrugged, but he shook my hand.

I want to be the same person with a crowd as I am alone.
- Lalit

qa.q: Where did Lalit go to field when the chant started again?
qa.a: He walked off to field at long-on, away from them.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel on stopping halfway through the chant?
qa.a: Lalit felt uneasy, because even though no one would pick out that voice, it was still Lalit's own, and the chant would come home too.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that others on the boundary could copy?
qa.a: He used his own words, 'Good ball, bowler,' walked away when the group kept going, and apologised to Santosh after the match.

qa.q: How might Santosh have experienced the match from the bowling crease?
qa.a: He faced a whole boundary mocking his body, which is hard to answer, so a single honest apology may have meant more than the shrug showed.

grounding: A young man stops himself joining a crowd's taunts, uses his own words, steps back, and apologises, staying accountable when he could hide in the group.

passage: When Coach Lind made Oskar captain of the under-sixteen handball team in Gothenburg, he got an armband and the keys to the ball cupboard. By the third week he was a different player. He changed Tuesday practice to seven in the morning without asking anyone, because it suited his piano lessons. He made the younger boys collect all the balls while he practised penalties. When Sofia said that the new time meant she had to skip breakfast and cycle in the dark, Oskar didn't even stop bouncing the ball. "Captain decides. If you want to play, you come." A couple of the boys laughed. Oskar liked that, and liked how people moved when he pointed. He didn't notice that Sofia had stopped passing to him in practice.

qa.q: Why did Oskar move Tuesday practice to seven in the morning?
qa.a: Because it suited his piano lessons.

qa.q: How does Oskar feel about being obeyed, and what shows it?
qa.a: He enjoys being obeyed, liking how the boys laughed at his line and how people moved when he pointed.

qa.q: What could Oskar have done when Sofia raised her problem?
qa.a: He could have stopped, listened, and asked the whole team which practice time worked, instead of dismissing her.

qa.q: How does Sofia see Oskar's captaincy?
qa.a: She sees a captain who ignores her needs, skipping breakfast and cycling in the dark, and her not passing to him shows she has lost trust in him.

grounding: A teenage boy made captain starts bossing teammates, enjoys being obeyed and brushes off a complaint, caring only about his own schedule.

passage: The school library had a new prefect badge, and Aparna, fourteen, wore it pinned exactly in the centre of her pocket. At first she was helpful. By the second month, the library felt like her room. She moved the Class 7 students to the hard benches by the window so her friends could have the soft chairs. She started fining people a rupee for whispering, even when they were asking where a book was. When Akash said the fine was unfair because the librarian had never charged anything, Aparna tapped the badge. "The librarian put me in charge." She wrote his name in her notebook. Watching him leave, she felt a small satisfying click, like a door shutting. She didn't think about why fewer students came in at lunch.

qa.q: What did Aparna start fining people for?
qa.a: She started fining people a rupee for whispering.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she wrote Akash's name in her notebook?
qa.a: She felt a small satisfying click, which shows she enjoyed her power more than caring about his point.

qa.q: What could Aparna do if she wanted the library to feel fair again?
qa.a: She could ask the librarian and the students what the rules should be, drop the fine and share the soft chairs instead of keeping them for friends.

qa.q: How might the Class 7 students see the library now?
qa.a: They may feel pushed aside and unwelcome, which could explain why fewer students come in at lunch.

grounding: A teenage library prefect grows bossy with her small authority, enjoys being obeyed and dismisses a fair complaint.

passage: I'm Harish. In my third year of college I was made senior under-officer at the NCC camp. It was the proudest day of my life, and I'm only now seeing what came after. I stopped noticing the juniors' faces. When Ojas, a first-year, said, "Sir, my blisters are bleeding, can I skip one drill?" I told him, "Blisters build character," and moved on. The same week I skipped the cold dawn run myself, twice, telling myself I had admin work. I took the only bunk near the heater. If you had asked me then, I would have sworn I was the same easygoing Harish who used to share my blanket on the train. It was Ojas limping at the passing-out parade that finally made me see it. Too late for his feet.

qa.q: Why did Ojas ask to skip one drill?
qa.a: Because his blisters were bleeding.

qa.q: How did Harish see himself during the camp, and what shows the gap?
qa.a: He believed he was still the same easygoing person, yet he dismissed Ojas's blisters and bent the rules for himself by skipping the dawn run and taking the bunk near the heater.

qa.q: What could Harish have done differently when Ojas asked to skip the drill?
qa.a: He could have looked at the blisters, let Ojas rest or see the camp medic, and followed the same rules he set for others.

qa.q: What was the camp like for Ojas under Harish?
qa.a: Ojas felt unheard and in pain, having to keep drilling with bleeding feet while his senior skipped runs himself.

grounding: A student given rank at camp becomes less attentive to a junior's pain and bends rules for himself, without noticing the change.

passage:
Lab manager's note, 18 July. Written by Mrs Nair.

Yogesh, twenty-one, was made lead of our summer intern batch three weeks ago. He's capable, and I chose him for his friendliness. Since then I've seen some changes. He gave himself the only fast computer and left early two Fridays while the others stayed to finish sample logs. When Dhruv, the youngest intern, asked for help with a calibration he had never done, Yogesh said, "Read the manual, I learned it alone," and put his headphones back on. Dhruv redid the calibration three times and missed his train.

When I raised this, Yogesh looked genuinely surprised. "Ma'am, I'm the same as always. I just have more responsibility now." I believe he means it.

My next step: a short weekly meeting where each intern, Dhruv included, tells me one thing that helped and one that didn't, with Yogesh present.

qa.q: What did Yogesh give himself after becoming lead?
qa.a: He gave himself the only fast computer.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh look surprised when Mrs Nair raised the problem?
qa.a: He genuinely believed he was the same as always and had not noticed he was bending rules and ignoring juniors.

qa.q: Why could the weekly meeting help Yogesh?
qa.a: Hearing what did and didn't help from the interns themselves would show him how juniors feel, which his new role has made him stop noticing.

qa.q: How did Yogesh's change affect Dhruv?
qa.a: Dhruv was left to struggle alone with a calibration he had never done, redid it three times and missed his train.

grounding: A new intern lead grows less attentive to juniors and bends rules for himself, while sincerely believing he has not changed.

passage: "Naveen, you've been in front of that mirror for ten minutes." Suraj leaned on the bathroom door. "I'm practising. 'Sir, I have a small suggestion.' No. 'Sir, if you have a moment.' No." "For what?" "The client proposal. My numbers are better than his." "So tell him." Naveen laughed without humour. "You don't know Bhatia sir. If he comes in whistling, you can speak. If he takes his glasses off, you say, 'Yes sir, very good sir.'" "And today?" "Glasses off." "So you said nothing." "I said his plan was excellent." Suraj was quiet. "Bhaiya, at college you argued with the dean." "That was college." Naveen rinsed his face. "Now I just watch his glasses." "You've gone smaller," Suraj said. "Since you joined." Naveen looked at himself in the mirror and didn't answer.

qa.q: What does Bhatia sir do when Naveen should say only 'Yes sir'?
qa.a: He takes his glasses off.

qa.q: What does Naveen's rehearsing in the mirror suggest about how he feels at work?
qa.a: It suggests he feels nervous and watchful, so unsure of his boss's mood that he has to practise even a small suggestion.

qa.q: What small step could Naveen take with his better numbers?
qa.a: He could send the numbers in a short written note, so his idea is on record even on a 'glasses off' day.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the change in his older brother?
qa.a: Suraj sees that Naveen, who once argued with the dean, has become quieter and smaller since joining this job.

grounding: A young employee learns to read his boss's moods and say only what pleases, and his brother sees him shrinking.

passage: I'm Yamini. At twenty-four I got my first cook's job in Vaibhav Chef's restaurant kitchen, and I learned to read him before I learned his recipes. If he tied his apron twice round, the day was fine. If he came in with it hanging loose, nobody spoke unless spoken to. I had ideas. I thought the dal could use less cream, and I knew the order system wasted food. I said none of it. On good days he called me beti. When he asked, "Any problems?" I said, "No, Chef." I tasted my own cooking less and his mood more. After a year, a new girl asked me what I thought of the menu, and I opened my mouth and realised I didn't know. I'd been so busy watching the apron that I had stopped having opinions. I felt about half my size.

qa.q: What did it mean when Vaibhav Chef tied his apron twice round?
qa.a: It meant the day was fine.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel after a year in that kitchen, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt small and lost, since she could not answer the new girl's question and felt about half her size.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and what could she do next?
qa.a: Being asked her opinion and finding she had none showed her how much she had hidden; she could start by writing down one idea a week and sharing it on a good day.

qa.q: How might the new girl see Yamini when she cannot answer?
qa.a: The new girl might be surprised, expecting a cook with a year's experience to have clear views on the menu.

grounding: A young cook learns to read a powerful chef's moods and hide her views, and slowly feels smaller.

passage: At the milk cooperative in Wadgaon, Yusuf had always been the joker who helped everyone carry the cans. Then, at twenty-five, he was made collection-centre supervisor. Reena, who tested fat content at the next table, watched him change over two months. He began cutting farmers off mid-sentence when they queried a reading. He expected the first glass of tea from the stall boy, before the women who had been standing since five. In the meeting he talked over her twice. The other staff whispered about it by the chilling tank. Reena didn't join them. She also knew the dairy board now phoned him every evening about falling numbers. One afternoon, walking to the bus stand, she said, "Yusuf, you've stopped letting people finish. I think the board's pressure is getting to you, but the farmers feel it." He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "Stop me when I do it."

qa.q: What was Reena's job at the cooperative?
qa.a: She tested fat content at the next table.

qa.q: What did Reena do well when she spoke to Yusuf?
qa.a: She named one clear behaviour, linked it to the pressure he was under, and said it privately on the walk, so he could listen without losing face.

qa.a: They are cut off when they question a reading and see the women who waited since five served tea last, which likely feels unfair and disrespectful.

grounding: A colleague notices a friend-turned-supervisor interrupting and expecting special treatment, and gently names it while recognising the pressure on him.

passage:
Monday, week one. Hrithik, twenty-five, was made site lead of a rooftop solar crew. At the first tea break he said, "I'm new at this. Tell me when I get it wrong," and handed out a slip of paper to each worker. Most came back blank.

Thursday, week three. The client wanted the job done by Sunday. Hrithik was ready to order Sunday work, then stopped and asked, "What does this cost you?" Pankaj, the oldest fitter, said flatly, "My son's school function." Two others had similar reasons. Hrithik moved two panels' work to Friday evening instead and asked Pankaj to keep telling him when he disagreed.

Saturday, week six. The company owner praised the fast job. Hrithik read out the names of every fitter, Pankaj first. That week, eight slips came back with writing on them.

qa.q: What did Hrithik hand out at the first tea break?
qa.a: He handed out a slip of paper to each worker.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik ask Pankaj to keep telling him when he disagreed?
qa.a: He seemed wary of drifting into giving orders without listening, and wanted to stay aware of what his decisions cost the crew.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how the crew responded to Hrithik?
qa.a: After he changed the Sunday plan and gave credit by name, the crew began to trust him, and eight slips came back with writing on them.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Hrithik after the Sunday decision?
qa.a: Pankaj might see a young lead who actually listens, which makes Pankaj more willing to speak honestly in the future.

grounding: A young site lead invites honest feedback, asks what decisions cost his crew, keeps a disagreeing voice close and shares credit.

passage: Sit, Anand. They made you team lead today, so let an old man tell you what I did when I got my first crew at the printing press. I was twenty-five, younger than most of them. Old Joseph, who ran the big machine, told me on my first day, "Everyone turns into a small king. Watch yourself." So I did three things. Every Friday I asked each man, "What did my decisions cost you this week?" Once it was a missed train, once a lost weekend. I fixed what I could. I kept Joseph close, even though he argued with me in front of everyone, and I thanked him for it. And when the owner praised a rush job, I said the names of the men who stayed up. Tarun Sir, they called me. I made sure it never went to my head.

qa.q: What did Old Joseph warn Tarun about on the first day?
qa.a: He said everyone turns into a small king and told him to watch himself.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep Joseph close even though Joseph argued with him?
qa.a: He wanted someone honest enough to disagree, because he was afraid of drifting into self-importance as Joseph had warned.

qa.q: Which of Tarun's habits might help Anand most in his new role, and why?
qa.a: Asking each week what Anand's decisions cost the team keeps Anand curious about the people below, so problems like a missed train get fixed.

qa.q: How might the crew have seen a young boss who named them in front of the owner?
qa.a: They would likely feel valued and trust him more, since he shared credit instead of taking it.

grounding: An elder remembers how, as a young leader, he asked for honest feedback, kept a disagreeing voice close and shared credit to avoid self-importance.
